title: A Multicenter Cohort Study Investigating Anxiety of Recurrence and Therapy-related Aspects in Patients with Early Breast Cancer
summary:
Many people diagnosed with breast cancer experience fear that their disease may return after treatment. This fear can significantly affect everyday life and well-being.

The study aims to investigate which personal, psychological and disease-related factors influence fear of cancer recurrence and how this fear changes over time.

Adult women and men diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer that has not spread to distant organs may participate.

Over a period of two years, participants complete questionnaires at seven predefined time points. These questionnaires assess their fears, emotional well-being, quality of life and coping with the disease. In addition, information about their disease and treatment is collected from medical records.

Medical treatment is provided independently of the study according to usual standards of care. No additional examinations or treatments are required.

The findings may help identify patients who need additional psychological support and improve future patient care.

interventions.name: Prospective observational cohort of patients with early breast cancer (stages I–III). Treatment is provided exclusively according to local standards of care. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Female and male patients aged 18 years or older.
2. Full understanding of the nature and scope of the study.
3. Confirmed breast cancer, stage I–III.
4. Known tumor subtype, including ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67, and type of (neo)adjuvant treatment.
5. No contraindications to potential chemotherapy or adjuvant radiotherapy.
6. Life expectancy of at least five years, independent of the cancer diagnosis.
7. Initial diagnosis after March 2026.
8. Known type of treating institution at initial diagnosis (university hospital, teaching hospital or oncology practice).
Exclusion criteria:
1. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or other preinvasive lesions.
2. Recurrent breast cancer.
3. Poorly controlled depression or history of inpatient psychiatric treatment.
4. Other psychiatric disorders, such as borderline personality disorder.
